entries.question: Are those who obey the law cursed?
entries.summary: Deuteronomy 27:26 places under curse anyone who fails to confirm and do all the words of the law, while Galatians 3:10 turns that same verse on its head, claiming that everyone who relies on the works of the law is under a curse.
entries.commentary:
Galatians 3:10 is one of the most discussed verses in Pauline studies because Paul appears to weaponize Deuteronomy 27:26 against itself. Deuteronomy 27:26 in the Hebrew curses anyone who *does not* uphold the words of the law. Paul quotes that verse — and concludes the exact opposite: that those who *are of* the works of the law are under a curse. The plain reading of Deuteronomy promises curse for non-compliance and (in chapter 28) blessing for compliance. The plain reading of Galatians 3:10 says compliance itself is the curse-trigger.

The major apologetic harmonization is the implicit-premise reading championed by N. T. Wright, Daniel Fuller, and others: Paul assumes nobody actually keeps the whole law, so the curse of Deuteronomy 27:26 falls on everyone who tries to be justified by it. On this reading, Paul isn't contradicting Deuteronomy — he's pointing out that the curse-clause of Deuteronomy gets triggered for everyone because perfect law-keeping is impossible. James Dunn's New Perspective version frames it differently: the curse falls on those who use the law as a boundary marker excluding Gentiles, not on Torah obedience per se. Either way, Paul is supposedly not actually contradicting Moses.

The Wright-Fuller implicit-premise reading does substantial work, and it's defensible at the level of Paul's argument. But it requires importing a premise Paul never states in Galatians 3:10 — that nobody can fulfill the law. Paul in fact contradicts that premise elsewhere; in Philippians 3:6 he calls himself "blameless" with respect to the law's righteousness. Heikki Räisänen and E. P. Sanders have argued at length that Paul's actual logic in Galatians 3:10 is genuinely strained — he is making rhetorical use of Deuteronomy 27:26 in a way the original Deuteronomic author would not have endorsed. Sanders' summary in *Paul, the Law, and the Jewish People* is blunt: Paul reaches his conclusion first (Christ is the basis of righteousness, therefore not the law) and then constructs a scriptural argument that runs against the surface meaning of the texts he cites.

The critical-scholarly verdict is mixed but lands where Sanders does. Whether you call this a flat contradiction or Paul "creatively reappropriating" Deuteronomy is partly a matter of how generous you want to be to Paul's hermeneutic. But the surface-level tension is real: Deuteronomy curses non-compliance, Paul effectively curses compliance, and reconciling them requires reading silent premises into Paul's argument. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence — but the unstated-premise solution sits awkwardly with Paul's own claim to law-blamelessness in Philippians 3.

commentary_out.commentary:
Galatians 3:10 is among the most analyzed verses in Pauline studies because Paul appears to turn Deuteronomy 27:26 against the very law it defends. Deuteronomy 27:26 closes the Shechem curse-liturgy: "Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them." Here the textual situation matters, and it is the standard scholarly explanation of Paul's wording. The Masoretic Text reads simply *et-divrei ha-torah ha-zot* ("the words of this law") without the quantifier *kol* ("all"), whereas the Septuagint reads πᾶσιν τοῖς λόγοις ("all the words") and the Samaritan Pentateuch likewise has "all." Paul's citation in Galatians 3:10b — "Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all things written in the book of the law" — reflects this "all" reading; commentators on Galatians regularly note that the emphatic πᾶσιν is precisely what lets Paul raise the bar to comprehensive, faultless compliance. His wording, however, is an adaptation rather than a verbatim Septuagint quotation: he conflates Deuteronomy 27:26 with phraseology echoing Deuteronomy 28:58 and 29:20 ("written in the book of the law"), producing a composite citation that serves his syllogism.

Paul's premise (3:10a) is the reverse of Deuteronomy's plain force: "as many as are of the works of the law are under a curse." On the surface Deuteronomy promises curse for *non*-compliance (with blessing for compliance in ch. 28), while Paul deploys the same verse to place those who *rely* on law-compliance under curse.

The logical gap is the famous "missing premise." Paul's syllogism only works if one supplies an unstated middle term — that no one in fact keeps the whole law, so the curse of Deuteronomy 27:26 falls on all who attempt justification by it. N. T. Wright, Daniel Fuller, and many others reconstruct exactly this: Paul is not contradicting Deuteronomy but invoking its own curse-sanction against a humanity that cannot meet the "all things" standard. James Dunn's New Perspective variant relocates the curse — it falls not on Torah-obedience as such but on the law used as an ethnic boundary marker excluding Gentiles, so Paul critiques covenantal exclusivism, not Torah-keeping. Both forms are exegetically serious and cohere with Paul's surrounding argument, where he immediately cites Habakkuk 2:4 and Leviticus 18:5 in 3:11-12 to oppose faith and law as competing principles of life.

The implicit-premise reading does substantial exegetical work and is defensible at the level of Paul's rhetoric. But it requires importing a premise Paul never states in Galatians and which he elsewhere appears to deny: in Philippians 3:6 Paul calls himself, "as to righteousness under the law, blameless" (ἄμεμπτος) — implying the law *can* be kept at the relevant level. If perfect law-keeping were impossible by definition, that self-description would be incoherent. E. P. Sanders and Heikki Räisänen press exactly this point. Sanders's verdict in *Paul, the Law, and the Jewish People* (the key "reasoning backward" discussion falls in the law chapter, roughly pp. 20-25 of the 1983 Fortress edition) is that Paul reasons backward: convinced first that righteousness is in Christ (and therefore *not* in the law), he then assembles scriptural proofs that strain against their plain sense. The Deuteronomic curse was a sanction for covenant infidelity, not a verdict on the whole enterprise of Torah; Paul re-reads it midrashically to serve a conclusion the Deuteronomist would not recognize. Räisänen documents the resulting inconsistencies across the Pauline corpus, treating Galatians 3:10 as one node in a pattern rather than an isolated slip.

Hans Dieter Betz and Martinus de Boer treat Galatians 3:10 as a deliberate, rhetorically charged reappropriation rather than neutral exegesis — Betz reading the verse within the forensic-rhetorical architecture of the letter, de Boer within Paul's apocalyptic antithesis between the present evil age and the new creation. Tigay's reading of Deuteronomy 27 underscores the point from the Hebrew side: the dodecalogue of curses at Shechem is a covenant-ratification liturgy targeting specific covenant breaches, not a meditation on the impossibility of obedience. The Deuteronomic curse presupposes that obedience is achievable — "this commandment is not too hard for you" (Deut 30:11) — which is the inverse of the premise Paul's argument requires.

Whether to call this a "contradiction" or a "creative reappropriation" is partly a judgment about how much hermeneutical license one grants Paul. The surface tension is undeniable — Deuteronomy curses non-compliance; Paul effectively curses reliance on compliance — and the standard harmonization rests on a silent premise that sits awkwardly with Philippians 3:6 and with Deuteronomy's own optimism about obedience. Hence "disputed." Verdict: real surface contradiction, resolvable only by importing an unstated and arguably un-Pauline premise about the impossibility of law-keeping.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The tension resolves only if one supplies Paul's unstated premise — that no one keeps the whole law, so Deuteronomy 27:26's curse falls on all who seek justification by it (Wright, Fuller) — but that premise is nowhere stated in Galatians 3:10 and sits awkwardly with Paul's claim to law-blamelessness in Philippians 3:6, which is why critical scholars (Sanders, Räisänen) read it as strained reappropriation rather than clean harmony.

issues.problem: The commentary and citation pin Sanders's 'reasoning backward' discussion to 'pp. 20-25' of the 1983 Fortress edition of *Paul, the Law, and the Jewish People*. Sanders's well-known argument that Paul reasons from solution (Christ) to plight is concentrated in the book's discussion of the law (roughly chapter 1, but the famous formulation appears around pp. 17-18 and 47-48), and a precise 'pp. 20-25' pin is not securely verifiable. The note even self-flags this ('page range verified against...the law chapter'), but presenting a specific page range as verified when it is uncertain overstates citation precision.
issues.correction: Either drop the specific page range (cite the work generally, e.g., 'Part One, on Paul reasoning from solution to plight') or hedge it explicitly ('approximately, in the discussion of Galatians 3:10–13') rather than asserting a verified pp. 20-25 pin.

entries.question: Who is the Lord of this world?
entries.books_in_tension: Joshua, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Ezra, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Micah, Zechariah, Matthew, Luke, John, Acts, 2 Corinthians
entries.summary: The Hebrew Bible repeatedly affirms YHWH as sovereign over all the kingdoms and the whole earth, but several New Testament passages — most notably the Temptation narrative and 2 Corinthians 4:4 — call Satan the "prince of this world" or "god of this world" with the kingdoms of the world apparently in his gift.
entries.commentary:
The Old Testament texts are univocal. From Joshua 2:11 through Psalm 47, Daniel 4:17, and Isaiah 37:16, YHWH alone is God of all the kingdoms of the earth. Then the New Testament drops in some startling counter-language. Matthew 4:8-9 and Luke 4:5-7 have Satan offer Jesus "all the kingdoms of the world," and crucially, Jesus does not deny Satan's possession of them — he refuses the deal on different grounds. John 12:31, 14:30, and 16:11 call Satan "the prince of this world" (*ho archon tou kosmou toutou*). 2 Corinthians 4:4 calls him "the god of this world" (*ho theos tou aionos toutou*). Ephesians 2:2 calls him "the prince of the power of the air."

The apologetic harmonization, defended by D. A. Carson and Murray J. Harris, distinguishes between *de jure* and *de facto* sovereignty. YHWH is the rightful king of the cosmos; Satan is a usurper currently exercising influence over the fallen world by divine permission. So God remains "Lord" in the metaphysical sense while Satan is the functional ruler of this present evil age — a temporary state that ends at the eschaton. Greg Boyd in *God at War* leans even harder into the warfare worldview, arguing the Bible consistently presents the cosmos as contested territory.

The two-tier sovereignty defense actually has Pauline support — Paul's apocalyptic framework (Rom 8:38, 1 Cor 2:8, Gal 1:4) does treat "this present evil age" as dominated by hostile powers under divine sufferance. So at the level of New Testament theology, this is a coherent move. But it doesn't actually map back onto the Hebrew Bible material, which simply doesn't have the *de jure / de facto* distinction. When Joshua 2:11 says YHWH is God in heaven above and earth beneath, the Deuteronomistic Historian is not setting up a category for "another god currently runs the kingdoms." The two-stage sovereignty is a theological development of the Second Temple period, not a feature of pre-exilic Israelite thought.

The critical-scholarly read places this contradiction inside the development of Jewish demonology. Paolo Sacchi, John J. Collins, and Larry Hurtado have traced how Second Temple apocalyptic — 1 Enoch, the Qumran Community Rule, *Jubilees* — developed an increasingly elaborate cosmic dualism in which fallen angelic powers (Belial, Mastema, eventually Satan) were assigned authority over the present age. The New Testament absorbs this apocalyptic framework, then applies it to Jesus' work. So "prince of this world" is not a reading you can extract from the Hebrew Bible; it's a Second Temple development that the New Testament authors retrofit onto older monotheistic claims. The Hebrew Bible says one thing, the Synoptics and Pauline corpus say another, and the harmonization works only if you privilege the later framework as a legitimate development rather than a contradiction.

commentary_out.commentary:
The Hebrew Bible texts are univocal on YHWH's universal sovereignty: from Joshua 2:11 ("YHWH your God, he is God in heaven above and on earth beneath") through 2 Kings 19:15, Psalm 47:2-7, Psalm 103:19 ("his kingdom rules over all"), and Isaiah 37:16 ("you alone of all the kingdoms of the earth"), no rival authority holds the nations. The New Testament then introduces startling counter-language. In the Temptation, Satan offers Jesus "all the kingdoms of the world and their glory" (Matt 4:8-9; Luke 4:5-7), and Luke 4:6 has him claim "it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will" — a claim Jesus refuses on other grounds without disputing the possession. John repeatedly titles Satan "the ruler of this world" (ὁ ἄρχων τοῦ κόσμου τούτου, John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11), and 2 Corinthians 4:4 calls him "the god of this age" (ὁ θεὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου) — the KJV renders αἰών here as "world," but the Greek term is properly "age," and that temporal sense is central to the harmonization below. Ephesians 2:2 names him "the ruler of the power of the air."

The apologetic harmonization (D. A. Carson, Murray Harris) distinguishes *de jure* from *de facto* sovereignty: YHWH is the rightful, ontological king of the cosmos, while Satan is a usurper exercising delegated, temporary, permitted influence over the fallen "present evil age," a regency that the eschaton terminates. Greg Boyd's *God at War* presses a thoroughgoing warfare worldview in which the cosmos is contested territory throughout Scripture.

This two-tier reading has genuine Pauline support and coheres internally within the New Testament. Paul's apocalyptic framework treats "this present evil age" (Gal 1:4) as dominated by hostile powers under divine sufferance: the "rulers of this age" crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor 2:8), and creation is subjected to bondage awaiting liberation (Rom 8:20-21, 38-39). The title "god of this age" in 2 Cor 4:4 is qualified temporally (τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου) precisely to mark a bounded, penultimate dominion, not an ontological rivalry to the Creator. At the level of New Testament theology, the *de jure/de facto* distinction is a coherent and arguably the intended reading. To that degree the tension is partially harmonized.

What the harmonization cannot do is read this two-stage sovereignty back into the Hebrew Bible. When Joshua 2:11 or Isaiah 37:16 affirms YHWH as God of all the kingdoms, the Deuteronomistic and Isaianic authors are not reserving a category for "another power that presently administers the nations." The bifurcated cosmic regency is a development of Second Temple Judaism, not a feature of pre-exilic Israelite thought. The earlier Hebrew Bible in fact knows a different model — the divine council of Deuteronomy 32:8-9, where in the Qumran (4QDeut-j) and the earliest recoverable Septuagint reading the Most High apportions the nations among "the sons of God" while keeping Israel as his own portion. The text-critical point should be stated precisely: 4QDeut-j reads בני אלהים ("sons of God") and the primary, oldest recoverable LXX reading is υἱῶν θεοῦ ("sons of God"), both against the MT's "sons of Israel" (בני ישראל), which is widely judged a theologically motivated revision; the reading ἀγγέλων θεοῦ ("angels of God") found in some Greek witnesses is a later, secondary harmonizing variant. Psalm 82 likewise has God judging the subordinate *elohim* of the nations. That council framework is closer to henotheistic administration than to a single satanic usurper, and it is itself distinct from the absolute monotheism of the Isaiah 37 / Psalm 47 affirmations, which signals development even within the Hebrew corpus. Mark S. Smith has reconstructed this trajectory from the Ugaritic divine-council background through Israel's emergent monotheism, making clear that the council model and the later cosmic dualism are successive, not identical, stages.

John J. Collins, Paolo Sacchi, and Larry Hurtado have traced how apocalyptic literature — the Watcher myth of 1 Enoch, the dualism of the Qumran Community Rule (1QS 3-4, the Two Spirits), and Jubilees with its figure of Mastema — progressively assigned fallen angelic powers (Belial, Mastema, eventually ὁ Σατανᾶς) authority over the present age. Hurtado's work is especially relevant because it shows that this elaboration of hostile intermediary powers coexisted with, rather than displaced, a robust Jewish monotheism: subordinate powers could be granted bounded dominion without compromising the Creator's unique sovereignty. The New Testament inherits this framework and applies it Christologically, so that Satan's defeat is the inauguration of the age to come. "Ruler of this world" is therefore not extractable from the Hebrew Bible; it is a later cosmological development retrofitted onto older monotheistic affirmations. Verdict: internally harmonizable within the New Testament's de jure/de facto and two-ages scheme, but that scheme is a Second Temple development that does not exist in the Hebrew Bible texts cited, so the cross-testamental tension is real even where the NT-internal logic coheres.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Within the New Testament's apocalyptic two-ages framework, the de jure/de facto distinction (YHWH the rightful cosmic king; Satan a permitted, temporary usurper over 'this present evil age,' cf. Gal 1:4; 1 Cor 2:8; 2 Cor 4:4's temporal qualifier) coherently reconciles the titles — but that bifurcated cosmic regency is a Second Temple development absent from the Hebrew Bible texts cited, so it resolves the NT-internal tension without dissolving the cross-testamental one.

entries.question: What tribe was Aijalon from?
entries.summary: Joshua 21:23-24 lists Aijalon as a Levitical city given out of the tribe of Dan, while 1 Chronicles 6:66, 69 lists Aijalon as a Levitical city given out of the tribe of Ephraim.
entries.commentary:
Two parallel Levitical-city lists, two different parent tribes for Aijalon. Joshua 21:23-24: "And out of the tribe of Dan... Aijalon with her suburbs, Gathrimmon with her suburbs." 1 Chronicles 6:66, 69: "The tribe of Ephraim... Aijalon with her suburbs, and Gathrimmon with her suburbs." The Chronicler is clearly working from a parallel source to Joshua 21 — the city pairings, the formula, even the suburb-language are nearly identical — but the parent tribe attribution differs.

The apologetic harmonization runs the historical-shift reading. Sara Japhet and Roddy Braun in their Chronicles commentaries argue that Aijalon was originally Danite (matching Joshua 21) but later transferred to Ephraim's territorial control after the Danite migration north (Judges 18). Since Dan effectively abandoned its southern territory, Ephraim absorbed the surrounding cities, and the Chronicler — writing centuries later — accurately reflects the post-Danite-migration administrative reality. So both texts can be true, just at different historical moments.

The migration-shift read has actual textual support. Judges 18 does narrate Dan's mass migration north, and the southern Danite cities did revert to neighboring tribes. 1 Chronicles 7:24 places Ephraim's territory in the area surrounding Aijalon. The Chronicler is well-known for updating geographical and administrative information from his sources to reflect later realities. So the reading isn't ad hoc.

Where it gets shakier is the textual-criticism dimension. The tribal lists in Joshua 21 and 1 Chronicles 6 are widely understood as variants of a single underlying source document. Sara Japhet's *I & II Chronicles* commentary in OTL and the textual notes in Steven McKenzie's commentary both observe that the two lists also disagree on the parent tribe of Gath-rimmon — Joshua 21:25 has it from the half-tribe of Manasseh while 1 Chron 6:69 (and apparently also the same context as Aijalon) has it from Ephraim. Plus the LXX of Joshua 21:24 has variants. So this isn't a clean "Joshua reflects period A, Chronicles reflects period B" sequence — it's two textually unstable lists with the kind of low-level corruption that scribal transmission of city-lists typically produces.

The critical-scholarly read combines both: the Levitical-city lists reflect an ideal program rather than continuously functioning administrative reality (Albrecht Alt, John Spencer), and the textual variants between Joshua 21 and 1 Chronicles 6 are partly real history (Dan's migration, Ephraim's expansion) and partly transmission errors. The contradiction is a real textual one even if the underlying administrative reality may have shifted; the historical-shift defense works in part but doesn't rescue the lists from being divergent witnesses to a fluid tradition.

commentary_out.commentary:
Two parallel Levitical-city lists assign Aijalon to two different parent tribes. Joshua 21:23-24 gives Aijalon (with Gath-rimmon) "out of the tribe of Dan." 1 Chronicles 6:66-69 places Aijalon (with Gath-rimmon) under "the tribe of Ephraim." The two lists are demonstrably parallel — the same city pairings, the same "with her suburbs" (*migrāsh*) formula — so the Chronicler is reworking either Joshua 21 or a shared underlying source, and the divergence in parent tribe stands out against that close agreement.

The harmonizing proposal, raised in connection with the Chronicles commentaries of Sara Japhet and Roddy Braun, is the historical-shift reading. Aijalon was originally Danite (so Joshua 21), but after the Danite migration northward narrated in Judges 18 — prompted by Dan's failure to hold its southern allotment (Judges 1:34) — the abandoned southern towns reverted to neighboring tribes, and Ephraim, whose territory bordered the Aijalon region, absorbed it. The Chronicler would then reflect this later administrative reality. This is not ad hoc: the Chronicler is well known for updating geographical and demographic detail in his sources, and Dan's migration is a real narrative datum. The reading carries genuine explanatory weight, which warrants partial harmonization. It should be said, however, that the migration-shift is more a harmonizing inference than the settled view of the commentators sometimes invoked for it: Japhet primarily treats Joshua 21 and 1 Chronicles 6 as variant textual witnesses to a single underlying document, not as cleanly dated period-A/period-B administrative snapshots, and Knoppers reads the relationship the same way.

Where the historical-shift reading weakens is the textual-critical dimension, because the divergence does not look like a clean period-A-versus-period-B sequence. The clearest symptom of transmission trouble lies in the very city paired with Aijalon. In the Masoretic Text Joshua 21:24-25 reads "Gath-rimmon" *twice* — once under Dan (v. 24) and again under the half-tribe of Manasseh (v. 25) — and the v. 25 repetition is universally recognized as a scribal dittography: the original at v. 25 was almost certainly "Bileam" (or "Ibleam"), the reading firmly preserved in the parallel list at 1 Chronicles 6:70 and supported by the Septuagint tradition (whose own witnesses here are divided, reading variant forms rather than a single clean "Bileam"). That is not random scrambling but a documented copyist error, and it sharpens rather than muddies the case: if the scribes who transmitted this block of Levitical-city material duplicated Gath-rimmon from v. 24 and lost the original name at v. 25, the divergent tribal assignment of Aijalon belongs to the same family of low-level corruptions. The well-known crux at Joshua 21:36-37 — where the trans-Jordanian Reubenite cities are absent in many Masoretic manuscripts and restored from the Greek and the 1 Chronicles 6 parallel — further illustrates, as a general matter, how unstable this entire list was in transmission, even though those Reubenite towns lie far from the Aijalon/Dan context and do not bear directly on it. Sara Japhet and the textual notes in Steven McKenzie's commentary accordingly treat the Joshua 21 and 1 Chronicles 6 lists as divergent witnesses to one underlying document whose copying introduced precisely this kind of corruption.

The critical-scholarly synthesis combines two factors. First, the Levitical-city institution itself is widely judged to reflect a literary-administrative program — possibly idealized or retrojected — rather than a continuously functioning system; Wellhausen treated priestly institutional material as late in his *Prolegomena*, Albrecht Alt analyzed its administrative geography, and John Spencer's study examined its role and historicity. Aharoni's geography places Aijalon precisely on the Dan-Ephraim frontier in the western foothills (the Aijalon valley guarding the approach to the central hill country), which is exactly the sort of border town whose tribal assignment would be fluid both on the ground and in transmission. Second, the specific Aijalon variant is plausibly part genuine history (Dan's migration, Ephraim's expansion into the vacated region) and part transmission error in a textually fluid list. The two explanations are not mutually exclusive: a real territorial shift could have been compounded by scribal instability of the kind the Gath-rimmon/Bileam dittography exposes.

The verdict is mixed. The historical-shift defense is the strongest available harmonization and accounts plausibly for why a once-Danite frontier town would later count as Ephraimite, so this is not a bare contradiction. But the recognized Gath-rimmon dittography and the documented textual instability of the Levitical-city lists show that the divergence is at least partly the product of imperfect transmission of a single source rather than two cleanly dated administrative snapshots. Verdict: partially harmonizable via Dan's migration, with residual textual corruption between two witnesses to one underlying list.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The Chronicler regularly updates source geography, and Aijalon plausibly passed from Danite to Ephraimite control after Dan's northward migration (Judges 18) left its southern towns to neighbors; this historical-shift reading accounts for the divergence in part, but the recognized Gath-rimmon dittography in Joshua 21:25 (MT, against the 1 Chron 6:70 'Bileam' parallel) and the broader textual instability show the two lists are primarily variant witnesses to a single underlying document, which is how Japhet and Knoppers chiefly frame them rather than as dated administrative snapshots.
